# fermi <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="120" alt="" />

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

fermi helps you make probabilistic estimates in R and Python using the [Fermi method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_problem). Break a complex problem into smaller variables and use Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the distribution of the outcome.

Whether you're estimating market size, the potential impacts of a policy change, or the number of piano tuners in Chicago, this tool provides a rigorous yet accessible way to handle uncertainty.

## Installation

Install the R package from GitHub.

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("humaniverse/fermi")
```

Install the Python package with Python 3.11 or newer.

```sh
python -m pip install "fermi-estimation @ git+https://github.com/humaniverse/fermi.git"
```

See the [Python guide](https://humaniverse.github.io/fermi/articles/python.html) for the same worked example in Python.

## Example

Let's say you want to estimate the annual number of dwelling fires in England. You can decompose this problem as follows:

$$
\text{number of dwelling fires} = \text{number of dwellings} \times \text{rate of dwelling fires}
$$

where `number of dwellings` can be further decomposed into:

$$
\text{number of dwellings} = \frac{\text{population}}{\text{average household size}}
$$

You can express your beliefs about each component using probability distributions (priors) and use `fermi` to estimate the expected annual number of dwelling fires.

```{r example, message=FALSE}
library(fermi)

# ---- Priors ----
# Population of England, which we'll judge to be between 54 and 56 million with 80% credibility
england_pop_prior <- expert_gamma_prior(
  q = c(5.4e7, 5.6e7),
  p = c(0.1, 0.9)
)

# Average number of people in a household, judged to be between 2 and 3.2 with 80% credibility
hh_size_prior <- expert_normal_prior(
  mean = 2.6,
  lower = 2.0,
  upper = 3.2,
  level = 0.8
)

# Risk of dwelling fires, judged to be between 0.01% and 0.06%, with 80% credibility
fire_rate_prior <- expert_beta_prior(
  q = c(0.0001, 0.0006),
  p = c(0.1, 0.9)
)

# ---- Fermi simulation ----
fermi_res <- bf_fermi_simulate(
  components = list(
    pop = england_pop_prior,
    hh_size = hh_size_prior,
    p_fire = fire_rate_prior
  ),
  # This is where we define how the components combine to give the final estimate
  fun = function(pop, hh_size, p_fire) {
    (pop / hh_size) * p_fire
  },
  n_draws = 20000
)

# Summarise and plot
posterior_summary(fermi_res, cred_level = 0.89)
bf_sensitivity(fermi_res)

plot_posterior(fermi_res, cred_level = 0.89)
```

Use `bf_compare_scenarios()` to compare estimates under different assumptions.
If you already have correlated draws from a model or bootstrap, pass them to
`bf_fermi_simulate()` as a data frame with one joint draw per row. To forecast a
future count or measurement from a conjugate posterior, use `bf_predict()`.

## Development

From the repository root, run `Rscript -e "testthat::test_local()"` to test R.
For Python, run `python -m pip install -e ".[test]"` and `python -m pytest`.
Both suites use the same cases in `tests/testthat/fixtures/parity/`.
